content.content:
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); a size is in the stamped class's name (`pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, `perf-probes/nat/java.md` § 1; `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`), and its descriptor in a stamped class is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics).
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below): this no longer holds. The checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters ("The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below), and a sized program loads and runs compiled ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).
- **The specification's own declaration of `Nothing` compiles on neither path, and the reason is name resolution, not codegen.** The Working Draft's `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:49`, kept in `Specification/basic-lib/convenience.tex:61-65` marked "Not allowed") stops on both paths with a syntax error at `excludes`, because the grammar gives an object no `excludes` clause (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:84-86`; `reviews/spec-refused-examples/probes/SpecNothing.fss` and its captures). Without that clause, `fortress compile` and `fortress walk` give the identical single error, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-maybe/probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss`, `.txt`; `reviews/spec-refused-examples/probes/SpecNothingNoExcludes.fss`). A where clause on an object declaration does not bind a type variable used in that declaration's extends clause in either implementation. `CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass` would refuse the declaration a second time at codegen — `header.getWhereClause().isNone()` is one of its `canCompile` conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:4093`) — but nothing reaches it. This is the mechanism behind the library's comment on its parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, "Obviously ought to be a non-parametric singleton when we get where clauses working" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1449-1450`), and it is why both worlds must spell the empty case some other way.
- **An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does when a component's name differs from the api it exports, and the failure is the repository's, not codegen's** (`compile-ladder/rung-export-var/`). Both paths assume an api and its implementing component share a name: `fortress link` and `walk` print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path", and the compiled run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The assumption is `Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`'s fallback to the api's own name (`linker/Linker.java:72-76`); only `LinkShell`'s `alink`/`clink` register another. The specification resolves an imported api to a component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex:33-35`), and the team reserved the codegen half in `CodeGen.java:411-441`, `:1856`, `:6599-6606`. Gated as an expected failure by `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test`.
- **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it** (`compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/probes/SpanAbsorb.fss` and `SpanAbsorb.txt`; ledger row 359). `createSpan` (`parser/Fortress.rats:145-157`) trims back over space characters only; a declaration ending in `end` is unaffected. So a comment-only library edit is not neutral at the syntax-tree level, and a before-and-after comparison of parse trees or diagnostics maps positions back first (`compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/parse-compare.sh`, `remap-lines.py`).
- **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees** (`compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-walk/REPORT.md`, section 4.1): `throw new FortressError((FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(name))` from a `builtinPrimitive` method reaches `Evaluator.forTry` unchanged; the helper is `Int.overflow()` (`interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:258-261`). Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`. The natives that raise `IntegerOverflow` so are those of "The interpreter's integer rules" and "Under `walk`, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when the result does not fit" under Landed semantics, with the narrowing checks `Int.rc` and `NN32.rc` (row 347 closed). Every other Java exception is mapped as before (`FunctionClosure.java:188-196`), so row 336's division by zero still ends the run.
- **The compiled run's class loader takes its first load of a name under the JDK's class-loading lock, and a generic arm's first load is safe on four threads** (`compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1, 11, 12; row 417). `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` runs under `getClassLoadingLock(name)`, as the JDK's `ClassLoader.loadClass` does; no loader in the tree registers as parallel-capable, so the lock is the loader's own monitor, and the explicit loads (`RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`, `RTHelpers.getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) are under it too. Gated by `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` in the gate's four-thread stage.
- **Walk chooses between a generic declaration and another on their declared domains, so the order they are written in no longer decides** (`compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 5.1; POSITIONS, "The static-parameter sentence goes"; row 548). `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchInternal` keeps a candidate by `moreSpecificDeclaration` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:1420-1427`): beside a generic function or constructor the declared domains are compared through the symbolic instantiation (`instanceHolding`, `:1376-1391`), otherwise the instances' domains; a generic trait's functional method and a generic dotted method keep the instance comparison. A chosen generic instance that converts an argument dispatches again (`convertedCall`, `:1307-1324`), not for overloaded methods. The symbolic instantiation is keyed by each static parameter's kind and bounds (`GenericFunctionOrMethod.java:57-68`; row 478, fixed), not by a `where` clause (`FGenericFunction.java:49-51`). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss`, `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss` and `GenericOverloadBoundsApart.fss`.
- **Walk's load check reads a generic declaration beside a plain one on declared domains, and covers an overlap through `comprises` clauses, where its parameter-by-parameter check refuses** (`compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 and 5.4; POSITIONS, "Conversions never change which declaration runs" and "The `comprises` passages read at the level of values (PLAN item 26, row 491)"; row 492, fixed). Both run only where the parameter-by-parameter check refuses (`OverloadedFunction.java:497-500`). For one own generic beside a plain declaration, `validOnDeclaredDomains` (`:693-722`) compares declared domains under the return-type rule and accepts an overlap that plain declarations below both cover, reading each parameter of the generic as the types whose intersection holds its values: a type parameter as its bounds that name no static parameter, a type that mentions a static parameter as `Any`, a non-type static parameter as no reason to refuse (`genericOverlapCovered`, `:728-778`; `intersectionPieces`, `:917-976`; row 552, fixed); for two plain declarations with an unrelated parameter pair, `overlapCovered` (`:814-825`; `overlapPieces`, `:986-1030`) cuts the overlap by the `comprises` clauses and needs every part inside one declaration below both, refusing what it cannot settle. Two generic declarations take the parameter-by-parameter check alone (Q4 = (1)). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss`, `ComprisesCoverReturn.fss`, `GenericBesidePlainTwoBounds.fss` and `GenericBesidePlainOverlapShapes.fss` (row 552), and the refusals `XXXGenericBesidePlainReturnRule.fss`, `XXXComprisesMeetUncovered`, `XXXComprisesCoverReturnWrong` and `XXXOverloadExistentialMeetWalk.fss` (row 539). Walk checks the closure of the main component's `comprises` clauses (row 551), not yet the library's (rows 595, 596), another component's (row 551) or an object expression's (row 597; "Walk checks at load the `comprises` clauses of the program's main component ..." below).
- **Walk instantiates a generic declaration declared to return `Any`** (`compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 3; row 157, fixed): `MakeInferenceSpecific.forAnyType` is a no-op like `forTraitType` (`interpreter/evaluator/MakeInferenceSpecific.java:72-75`). Gated by `tests/GenericReturningAny.fss`; row 496's probe `PlainBesideZZ32` prints `Marker[ZZ32]` under walk. The visitor has no case for 11 of the AST's 18 concrete type classes, of which only the dimension forms can be written as a return type.
- **Walk checks at load the `comprises` clauses of the program's main component, and its harness names an expected refusal at load** (`compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md`; row 552 fixed, row 551 for the main component's clauses). `BuildEnvironments.checkComprisesClauses`, called from `Driver.evalComponent` once every component's types are built, reads the declarations as written and asks every extender of a closed trait of the main component for the traits chapter's three eligible forms, reading a generic child's extenders across the whole program; the library's clauses (rows 595, 596), another component's (row 551), an object expression (row 597) and the clause's other half, that a listed type extends each instantiation (row 598), are not read. A file `Name.fss` of `tests/` names its refusal in `Name.test` by `load_exception_contains` (`FileTests.java`, `InterpreterTest.loadRefusalKeys`): a plain test passes when walk refuses the program at load as named, an `XXX` test when the program loads and runs clean; a failure while the top-level variables are initialized counts as a refusal at load. Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender`, `ComprisesGenericChildUnlistedExtender`, `GenericBesidePlainOverlapShapes` and the `XXX` files of rows 22, 487, 534, 544, 549, 597 and 598.

content.content:
## The checker and the one library

- The one library binds its natives with `builtinPrimitive("…")`: 424 live bindings in nine files (445 written, 20 inside comments, one `RR32` binding fewer since `RR32` became a sibling of `RR64`), 125 of them in `FortressLibrary.fss`, and the rest of the library is plain Fortress. Beside them, walk loads the Java classes of 32 objects of `native component`s by name and binds `true`, `false` and `Any` at start-up. The interpreter's glue classes take the evaluator's boxed values and cannot be reused by the compiled path; the compiler's natives are static Java methods over plain Java values, called through `import java`: 369 public static helpers in 25 classes of `nativeHelpers/`, which the compiler prelude's 366 native bodies call. Matched by owner, name and signature, then by operation: 147 of the bindings are bound on the compiled path already, so only their binding text changes; 61 have a helper that nothing binds yet, 25 of them under a name the compiler prelude binds to another helper, the 12 wrapping operators among them (row 348); 139 need a new static helper, written from 132 glue classes of about 0.7K lines; and 78 need something else, 36 methods of native I/O objects (`Writer`, `BufferedWriter`, `FileReadStream`, `FileWriteStream`, `Reader`) and 42 with no compiled analogue (reflection, `Thread`, the native arrays, the task trace). The prelude and what it imports hold 369 of the bindings. Every program's output needs the I/O objects: `println` writes through `stdOut`, a native `Writer` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4340-4343`, `Library/Writer.fss:20-24`), so the first compiled program on the one library needs `Writer`'s natives. MicroGPT calls `nanoTime`, which needs a new helper (the compiled one returns `RR64`), imports `System`, whose top-level `args` cal
- `fortress compile Library/FortressLibrary.fss` as it is: 1,417 errors, all in DISAMBIGUATE, all name collisions because both preludes are in scope; an artifact. With `FortressLibrary` made the prelude (a driver over `Shell`'s public entry points, no tracked file changed), disambiguation passes with zero errors (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`). What the checker then reports on the library, which the gate's checker-count and distance stages measure at every landing, is in "The true distance to the switch-over" below; it checks `nat` and `int` static parameters and refuses a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` one by name, with no crash ("The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below).
- **The Scala type checker does not implement `nat` static parameters at all** does not hold: the checker implements `nat` and `int` static parameters, a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` one has a named error, not rules ("The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below), and a sized program runs compiled ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics). The title was the first measurement of the checker against the library (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`).
- **Between the interpreter's library and bytecode stands the checker, not desugaring or code generation** (`perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md`, the library pushed through DESUGAR and CODEGEN with the checker's failures caught per top-level declaration, validated on `CompilerLibrary.fss` where the method reproduces the ordinary compile exactly). On the nested tower, of `FortressLibrary.fss`'s 446 top-level declarations the checker passed 237 clean, reported errors on 97 and crashed on 112 (81 `makeInferenceArg` nyi, 29 `TraitType→IntExpr`, the `nat` gap, both since closed); DESUGAR and OVERLOADREWRITE then report zero diagnostics on all of it; CODEGEN emitted 275 and refused 313, of which only **5 were on declarations the checker checked clean** (four a numeric static argument, one a method call on an intersection-typed receiver); the rest were missing annotations on unchecked declarations (227), `Juxt` (53), the checker's shadow rather than a missing visitor (a juxtaposition is what the checker resolves into an application or a method call, and all 53 were on declarations it crashed on or refused, `desugar-codegen.md` § 2.2, § 6), the missing visitor `Label` (1), `nat` static arguments (14), malformed overload sets (7); `canCompile` refused nothing and no native binding was missing. Two obstacles the error counts do not show: the compile path's own `extends Object` pre-desugaring (`Shell.java:371-386`) adds 712 of the 960 checker errors in the prelude apis and 618 of 1,204 in the component under its own setting, rejecting every generic instantiated at a tuple type (row 412; the gate's stages run under the bound `Any` instead); and overload dispatch generation did not terminate on the nested library's exclusion graph (1,046 s, stopped by hand). On the flat libr
- **The `nat` plan's minimal design works as a shadow, and the road is three batches, not one** (`perf-probes/nat/REPORT.md`, `shadow.patch`, 22 captures): the design is built, the checker half as "The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below and the run-time half as "A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics. What the shadow established that still describes the tree: a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` static parameter gives a checker error naming the kind; the size crash had a Java site as well as a Scala one (`compiler/codegen/FnNameInfo.java`, any method on a nat-parameterized receiver), and a compiled sized program needs a run-time kind for sizes, since `isOprKind` (`Naming.java:103`) is the run time's only other static-argument kind predicate; the api has 25 declarations with a dead size (E3, POSITIONS, "Sizes"), and the per-declaration check of `trait Number` alone takes minutes without the trait table's memo ("`TypeAnalyzer.parents` and `excludesClause` are memoized per trait table" below).
- **The shadow's two `subarray` errors were the rule's, fixed in two lines, and the checker's slowdown is the tree's own** (`perf-probes/nat/followup.md`, captures `followup/`). A size left unsolved after comparing two declarations' return types was counted as a failure (`Formula.imp`, `Formula.scala:168`, via `OverloadingOracle.satisfiesReturnTypeRule` and `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:145`); the two-line relaxation there proved unneeded, `keep-size-params` alone clearing the `subarray` refusal ("The return-type rule now reads a size as it reads a type parameter" below); the denied shape was `Vector`'s, `Matrix`'s and C4's slicing, so the rule carries it. The slowdown: 87 % of 39,287 JFR samples in `TypeAnalyzerUtil.substitute` from `TypeAnalyzer.parents` (`:722`) and `excludesClause` (`:747`), the second recursing over every supertrait, no sample in the size track; the memo that removes it lives on `TraitTable` ("`TypeAnalyzer.parents` and `excludesClause` are memoized per trait table" below). Five declarations of the library report one error each under the size rule that they did not without it (`FortressLibrary.fss:129, :2248, :2594, :3064, :3151` at the shadow's lines), three of one shape (a `__bigOperatorSugar` body whose return type is taken from the nullary api overload, `.fsi:96` not `:98`, no size in them) and `__builtinFactory2` a likely true positive (branches `Array2[\T,0,s0,0,s1\]` and `__DefaultArray2[\T,b0,s0,b1,s1\]` join only under its own `if b0=0 AND b1=0` guard); they are read in the distance stage's table, not re-traced.
- **The Java site of the size crash is nine lines, and a sized program runs compiled with a stamped descriptor per literal** (`perf-probes/nat/java.md`, `java/java-shadow.patch`, captures `java/`). `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` (`compiler/codegen/FnNameInfo.java:162-173`) returned a `TypeArg` for every static-parameter kind; with `KindNat`/`KindInt` mapped to `IntArg(IntRef name)`, the identity `STypesUtil.staticParamToArg` already gives (`STypesUtil.scala:338-339`), every `cannot be cast to IntExpr` crash is gone (built as kind-correct static arguments in `FnNameInfo.boundsFor`, "The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below). `bool`, `dim`, `unit` and `opr` keep the latent `boundsFor` bug, which still returns a type argument for every kind but `nat` and `int` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/FnNameInfo.java:165-180`). The mangled name for a sized receiver keeps the size as its own symbol (`NamingCzar.forIntRef` `:1894-1897`, `forIntBase` `:1889-1892`). A descriptor is asked for at `MethodInstantiater.rttiReference:117-138` and `CodeGen.generateTypeReference:5784-5793`; a symbol needs no descriptor (the template holds `Box⟦k⟧$RTTIc`), only literals reach the loader, and the landed `RTTIsize` (design B with the factory, POSITIONS, "The run-time size design is B") has no `javaRep`, the shadow's placeholder. The stamping tool `java/StampSizeRTTI.java` of the shadow is replaced by the factory. The gate cannot see a classpath shadow.
- **A size at run time can follow the opr path, 28 lines, and a size in value position is 25 more** (`perf-probes/nat/runtime.md`, `runtime/design-a.patch`, `runtime/value-position.patch`, captures `runtime/r1-r8`): design A, a size static argument exempted from needing an RTTI class the way `isOprKind` exempts oprs, is not taken (POSITIONS, "The run-time size design is B"); design B is built with the factory. What the probe established that still holds: the library's own source uses four size literals (0, 1, 2, 3) in 85 places; a size in value position is one `CONST` op in the substitute-at-load channel that the loader turns into an integer `LDC`, the specification's `makeVector` needing it not, the sentence beside it (`trait-parameters.tex:83-86`) and any array library needing it (built, "A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics); a type test on a size is an `INSTANCEOF` on the value's own class, also with the size a static parameter of the enclosing function; `pTypeCase` failing with the shadow off is row 340's shape, a `typecase` as a whole function body whose clauses need a coercion, and says nothing about generics (`reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` § 2). Design A's fourth gap (a size read inside a method of a sized object, expanded inside `Buf⟦3⟧$RTTIc` whose map does not bind `s`) is design A's own and does not exist under B.
- **The brief's three size probes, measured under both designs: design A's default falls to the brief's own stop condition, and the checker rung carries a four-line defect** (`perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md`, programs, patches and captures under `perf-probes/nat/size-probes/`). (1) A dispatched overload arm generic in a size (row 214's three arms with a catch-all, the argument typed `Any`): the checker's `normalizeUA` dropped every `nat` parameter from a generic arrow (`scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:449, 485`) and the return-type rule then compared two renamed sizes; four code lines fix it, landed as `keep-size-params` (row 410, closed). Past the checker, design A links, runs and silently picks the catch-all for every size-generic arm, because its dispatcher tests `INSTANCEOF Vec⟦FRR64,s⟧`, a class named with the arm's own symbol (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1015, 1077`); design B's dispatcher, as built, is right on all four programs and the arms read their sizes (`dispatch-b.patch` and its 14-line extends-clause piece, `extends-b.patch`; row 411). (2) Design A's fourth gap does not exist under B. (3) A type test on a size works under both designs, an `INSTANCEOF` on the value's own class. Also measured: row 366's program prints `Op[\+\]` on the stack, so design A's three `ONLY` lines are its fix (row 366 waits, POSITIONS, "The gate's comparisons"). Row 412, the compile path giving a size parameter `extends Object` (`compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:77-86, 135-148`), which B's dispatcher skips, is open; `DOT`'s shared size needs no fix ("The two probes before the run-time size rung" below).

- **The true distance to the switch-over, measured on today's tree: on the flat library the checker reports 1,736 distinct errors under walk's setting and 1,527 under the compile path's, of which the gate's count shows 62** (`perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat.md`, scripts and captures under `perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat/`; on the nested tower the totals were 2,523 and 2,359, `perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance.md`). The title's figures are that measurement's, on an earlier flat library. The last landed gate reads 253 under the gate's setting `any`, the bound `Any` with compiled-expression desugaring (POSITIONS, "The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`"), and a count of 1 (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-10/gate/distance.txt`, `checker-count.txt`, `summary.txt`); walk's setting and the compile path's own `extends Object` setting are not measured by the gate. Over twelve prelude apis and their twelve components, the overloading memo off, in one JVM (`DistanceMulti.java`), the 253 are: exclusion 0; `comprises` 0; overloading 2; return type 2; abstract method not implemented 8; the `extends Object` bound 0; other well-formedness 36; component bodies' type errors 201; export mismatches 4 (`distance.txt:3-11`; by root cause in the next entry). Each landed batch's movement by kind, unit and class is in its gate's `summary.txt`, its `distance` lines, and in its record's last section ("The landing" or "The gate"), under `compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/`. Three declarations crash the checker, `__bigOperator`'s local function ("Type is not inferred") and the untyped `fn` parameters in the rank-2 and rank-3 array traits, and so does `Stream`'s variance stage (`distance.txt:38-40`): three crash rows. Code generation, measured once by the title's measurement: `FortressLibrary` emits 326 declarations and refuses 225, 4 of them on declarations the checker passed; the overload rewriting's `BottomType` stop is gone; the dispatch generator finishes and refuses 12 of 198 overload sets (131 of 283 on the nested tower). The count stage runs walk's setting (by reading its code) and sees 1 of the distance's 253; its per-api rows count each error twice (`FortressLibrary` 2 against the total 1). The count stage runs the `FortressLibrary` api's overloading and return-type checks, which `StaticChecker` skips while a unit has an earlier error (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java:268-272`); the api's last early error, `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, is cleared ("The tower closure of `02d09a39f` has no spelling the compiler's checker accepts" below). Those checks add 1 error, the overloading of `isLeftZero` in `LexicographicReduction` (`compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`), counted twice and already counted by the distance stage. A zero count is necessary, not sufficient (`coordinator/library-route-judgement.md:33`). As a gate stage the one JVM matches the twelve separate runs within the variation; it is reported and never red, and compares with the last landed table (`last_landed_distance`, the gate's step 9, in `gateRole` of `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`); each landed batch's table is in its own gate directory, climb batch 7C's and N's in upper case. Its per-site list lands at one fixed path, `compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, overwritten at each landing (the commit stage's step 1), so that a rung whose test is this stage takes the landed tables as its before (POSITIONS, "No re-measuring what the record holds"); the batches landed before that practice have theirs beside their tables as `gate/distance-sites.tsv`. A run takes 786 to 1,212 s at a gate beside the other stages (each gate's `#seconds` row), 1,130 s under a load of 5.4 with `testFast` and a review beside it (`FortressLibrary` 784 s of it), and 14 to 24 minutes on a shared machine at load 7 to 18 (4 CPUs, Xeon 2.10 GHz, the 1,212 s at 2.80 GHz, JDK 25.0.4, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`). Runs vary by 2 to 4 errors, in big operators' bodies typed at their element and in the type a join infers for an array body (`compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-remainder/probes/distance-variation-base.txt`, `distance-variation-post.txt`, `compile-ladder/rung-tabulate/probes/distance-base-variation.txt`); repeated runs of one setup are identical site for site, and the varying families BR, V2 and O1 move between setups (the entry on the written bound `Object` below) and under edits that touch none of their declarations. Two such moves are attributed: the `comprises` rule's subtype queries in the hierarchy pass add the BR error at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1535` and respell or move three other body-check sites, the same in five runs of that build and absent under the broad form of the rule, which clears the same two H2 errors without the queries (`compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/probes/skeptic/distance-attribution.txt`); and the integer `MIN`/`MAX` declarations moved the family, touching none of its declarations, one BR site (`BIG MAXNUM`'s body) gone and `BIG //`'s body and a second error in `BIG SQCAP`'s body new, each message on file in distance tables before the edit (`compile-ladder/rung-integer-minmax/REPORT.md` section 8). The candidate cause, the trait table's memos keyed by `TraitType`, is ruled out: with them off the stage gives the same errors site for site (`reviews/row-488-probe.md`; "`TypeAnalyzer.parents` and `excludesClause` are memoized per trait table" below). The mechanism is not known (row 488, open). *Climb batch 10's rung G (`a9b9933e6`): every BR body site in `FortressLibrary.fss` that the landed lists and row 488 name was a big operator whose component declaration had no return type, the message naming the nullary overload's return type as the declared one; with the api's return type written on all eight (`BIG MIN`, `BIG MINNUM`, `BIG MAXNUM`, `BIG //`, `BIG ||`, `BIG AND`, `BIG SQCAP`, `BIG SQCUP` over a generator) the three such sites are gone and the calls `BIG MIN[\T\]()` print the one-argument candidate as `Generator[\T\]->T` where they printed `->BigReduction[\T,AnyMaybe\]` (`compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md` section 9).* *Climb batch 10's rung C (`aa07efb31`): three of the last landed table's four crash rows are one cause, a local function's omitted parameter type (rows 620 to 622; `compile-ladder/rung-checker-defects/REPORT.md` section 5), and the fourth, Stream's variance crash, is repaired (row 623), so the rung's tree shows three (section 8).*
- The checker-count stage's table, `gate/checker-count.txt`, lands with every batch beside the gate's `summary.txt`; `last_landed_checker_count` (the gate's step 8, in `gateRole` of `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`) finds the last landed table, the newest commit's under `compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/`: 1 at the last landed gate (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-10/gate/checker-count.txt`), with the `FortressLibrary` api's overloading and return-type checks counted ("The true distance to the switch-over" above). Each earlier batch's table is in its own gate directory, climb batch 7C's and N's in upper case. The table's `#cache` row names the stage's setting and is not an api (`coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh:93-94`). The total is reported and never red on its own, because a fix can raise it and two rungs' changes do not add; the gate stays red on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow or a table with no total (`checker_compare`, the gate's step 8), and the post-batch review ties every new or risen row to a named rung edit, reading the landed table (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing" and "The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage").

content.content:
### The standard and the sources

- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened by Steele in 2011, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
- **Fleshing out the standard library** is a very important task: first the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch (done by the flattening), then the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them; into the standard library itself, not a tree of our own.
- **Interpreter performance is irrelevant.** "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed, and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled. The two microGPT programs never run in the gate ("those are too long running to be tests"); the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
- **Development-loop performance is a first-class concern.** When an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
- **The territory map** (`coordinator/map/`) is the map down to where the design intent is written, papers as well as the specification; he wanted it before unsealing. The maps exist so that nothing on record is rediscovered; the boot order is followed as written, `INDEX.md` included.
- **The plan** (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) is six phases, approved with its workers: 1, the wrapping operators, the specification rung without the number chapters and the run-time size rung; 2, the flattening, the number chapters and the overflow natives; 3, the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code-generation holes; 6, microGPT fast. Phases 1 and 2 are landed. His answers come in the plan's order; the re-approval rows and the other off-path items are parked until relevant; row 41 joins the switch-over's design.

### The specification's revision

- **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people. We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C." Every change takes the S1 form, an original-tree edit flagged as such; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.
- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. The unrevised copy is called "the Working Draft of February 2011", in the team's own form, each citation giving the path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; Appendix I says once that the directory's name is misleading, since only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Appendix I's introduction says that the entries follow the revival's decisions, route A the first of them, each naming its own.
- **The refused examples (S2).** Each example the exclusion rule refuses is revised to the one library's shape, the original kept in the text as "Not allowed", the specification's own form, and the rule stated once in Luchangco's two-part form under "instantiation exclusion". Built. The `covariant` keyword gets one sentence in the revival callout at the covariance example, saying that the type group's later design declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, implemented on neither path, and pointing to the decision record and row 404. The number chapters (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, `basic-lib/numbers.tex`, `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`) changed in the same batch as the flattening, never earlier. The calculi of Appendix A (Core Fortress with Where Clauses, ACFFD and Basic Core) each carry a `\revision` callout saying that the calculus predates instantiation exclusion and admits the shapes the rule refuses, their rules and soundness claims untouched. The judgement's candidate ledger rows 2, 3 and 5 are parked (`PLAN.md`).
- **Appendix I's small items.** `TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]` in the api and the component, its five restated members kept, so that it gets back `MIN` and `MAX` (row 461 closed; built; taken on the coordinator's recommendation, and he wants it explained in more detail when he has the energy, "I need to pay that down", so it is on the list for his review).

### How we work

- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test.
- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.
- **Nothing is built or run twice on the same code.** "We don't want to re be rebuilding stuff that doesn't need to be rebuilt." The design, agreed with him and built into the batch script: the old code, the batch's base, is built once per batch, by the coordinator, before the launch, in a worktree nobody compiles or runs in (the script's `args.baseBuild`); "We just mechanically take the latest build and share it between each rung from the same baseline": every rung worktree is seeded from that one build in seconds (`coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean (his "Duh!" to "seeding a worktree by copying a built tree rather than rebuilding it"); the worker builds only what its own edit changed; the skeptic builds nothing, "very smart skeptics that just like reuse everything that was built during the rank phase as much as possible and just do their independent checks": it reads test-first from the worker's transcript, runs its own small programs on the new code with the rung's build and on the old code against the batch's one base build, through the rung's private seeded copy of it so that no two agents compile into one cache; the second skeptic checks only the repair against its own refusal; no stage re-runs a build, a suite or a measurement on a code state another stage has already run, and no agent reads again a log of output that has not changed: "I want to eliminate all waste of this type. Where we are re-executing stuff for no reason." How a worktree is seeded and what a worker clears after an edit or a failed build is engineering, measured before it is built into the batch script (`coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`; the blinded engineers' variants in `coordinator/process-engineering/cache-sharing.md`).
- **The coordinator watches what it launches.** Only a long or large run the coordinator launches outside a batch, a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more, is watched against the estimate it was launched with, so that none runs away as probe P1 did (`coordinator/process-engineering/p1-cost.md`); when it passes its estimate the coordinator reacts, by an instruction to the worker or a stop, and its brief carries what keeps it efficient, a wait polled under the prompt cache's life among it. Ordinary workers carry no such procedure, and no ask is added before a probe: "I don't want you to become paranoid about running probes"; "I don't want the cargo cult of ... monitoring here. Only longer runs. ... I don't want you to burden with ... procedure on each call to workers." P1's waste was one the worker knew how to avoid: "an instruction to that worker would have corrected it."
- **A deeper pass, not a halt.** When something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch, no bisection of commits: "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle, no stop: "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one." What reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
- **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
- **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
- **The mission briefing.** "this whole exercise is about in-context learning. You were not pre-trained on Fortress. And the language was not finished." The planner, who has the whole map, gives each rung a mission briefing from the map that its agents read in their first turn; the share of agents that use it is reported with each landing (it was about 80% once and fell to 25-35%: "We need to get back to that level"). The briefing is in neutral words, "the decisions on record" ("I am trying to stay humble and I don't want to see my name in there multiple times. Make this neutral."); the worker answers no required questions about its search ("I disagree with the procedural enforcement here ... it's giving the agent side quests that it's graded on instead of something that it should just take into consideration during the implementation"; the briefing says "this is not a Java, this is not a Scala, you are in unfamiliar territory", and then the worker "should focus on its tasks"); the skeptic checks the result against the library's way, the ledger and sibling sites, and the decisions on record.
- **No re-measuring what the record holds.** "you are wasting resources on remeasuring." A brief hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite and names the one new thing to measure; a clean worker is clean of our options, not of our measurements (protocol principle 5). A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before and does not re-run the stage on an unchanged base; the gate commits its per-site list so that the before is complete. The nine steps are a way to brief him on unfamiliar ground, a type-theoretical question answered from the theory, the rule and a few declarations; and one global rule is sought from type theory and the peers' implementations rather than a rule slapped on a rule ("I cannot be trusted to derive a rule that wouldn't break the whole system and be a hodgepodge of edge cases").
- **Reversible stops do not hold a batch.** A stop a batch record reserves for him (a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, an interpreter output a rung cannot account for): "These don't need me now. They are reversible things I can review later. Don't block start of next batches on these." It lands, the push and the next batch go ahead, and it is listed for his review (the protocol's first hard rule). An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop but a ledger row ("we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held"); a rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
- **A blocking second review does not hold a green batch.** "we have enough rigor or robustness and backup in our processes after that, so that small failure in a rule should not be blocking ... landing large ships like this." After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for his review, and the post-batch review follows. A red gate after its repair still stops a batch. Built into `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual. The merged-diff review itself stays inside the batch, once, beside the gate, as the check of the merged tree's records, the stops and the routing before the push; removing it and moving its checks to the review after the batch is not taken (Fable's review of the batch practice against the Opus review's; he sided with Fable).
- **A tests-only repair does not rerun the gate.** "we are being overly pedantic for no good reason with like how the gates are set up ... we have to be weighing costs and benefits and we are not skipping the test, we are adding the test, we are moving stuff to following batches, we are running reviews after the fact, so we will catch stuff that the rerunning of a gate is not." A repair after the gate that changes no source, library, checker, interpreter or specification file runs its new tests in the harness on the merged tree; the first gate's tables stand; the landing records the new tests beside them; a repair that changes code reruns the gate. The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to every rule of the batch workflow. Built.
- **What a batch commits.** "the commit discipline in a branch should not be different from what you will be committing to the main. Like don't keep temporary shit around. We are backing up the transcripts anyway from all the workers. So if we need to dig up something, how the worker arrived at some point, we have the full transcripts." A worker commits, on its own branch as on `main`, only what `main` is to hold: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script or tool that is reusable ("If that script that batch contributes a script that is reusable, it goes in there", such as the documented way of running the checker as a shadow); no captured outputs, logs, raw outputs, script copies or other scratch are committed anywhere; new issues go to the ledger, reports into the batch's report; the process, and whether a worker wrote its test first and saw it fail, is read from the workers' transcripts, which the backup keeps. Deleting the `wip/` branches after a gate is his own chore in the GitHub web page, and he is not reminded of it. Built into the script, its manual and the protocol.
- **Workers commit their own files as they go.** "Workers should be committing themselves as they go, focused their files only. Protects against container failures and stops from harness bothering you about uncommitted files." They push to their own `wip/` branches as they work; the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the coordinator pushes `main` every few minutes ("I hope we are committing as we go because I worry that the container will get reset"). A protocol hard rule.
- **Which tier runs what.** "You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." The highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier, because that is the work it is for. Workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof"; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls". Sonnet is the tier for archaeology. Two workers launched on the wrong tier once cost him 1.7 million tokens "down the drain". The coordinating session runs on Opus, so that Fable's own weekly pool is kept "for more important work"; it moves to Fable at his word when the pool on all models is spent, and how the Opus trial is judged is in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`.
- **The judge's rulings.** A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable ("Second ruling is for Fable."), named in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` (`judgeTier`), so Fable is spent only when a second ruling happens. The review's judge rules while the gate runs on, and the gate writes its outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage. A second repair round is not taken; option (b), approvals with required corrections when the fix is already written, has not been put to him (parked, `PLAN.md`).
- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
- **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
- **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s: batch 8 next. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
- **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
- **Check-ins and stops.** A series of check-ins is spaced 45 minutes apart, since hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price; the one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
- **Where the work lives.** The work runs in the container on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it; transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded`, "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts?", and the lineages are joined at analysis time; the container recovery procedure is a lesson about the remote container (`coordinator/remote-container.md`), not a ledger row. Everything of ours is under `explorations/` ("to remove confusion for any workers"); the inventory note's own move list waits on his reading (parked, `PLAN.md`). Later, a cleaner pass: `main` holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, the whole process record lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of `main` with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress; GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches. A post-mortem index points into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that regenerates any verbatim view; the transcript is not restated.
- **The record is public and names models on purpose.** The protocol's rule against model identifiers is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here.
- **The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.** FACTS and POSITIONS are the optimized build, "what is true about the repository snapshot at this moment in time", written timelessly: no dates, no provenance, no account of what changed when or what corrected what; the history files are the debug build, with the full provenance, his quotes at their dates and every earlier text. "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." A worker or a coordinator appending to FACTS or POSITIONS needs no timestamps; where one is written, or an entry corrects an earlier one, the next consolidation moves that provenance into the history and rewrites the fact or the position without it, at full informational fidelity. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since workers read it and pay the cost. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, and the rung entries already in the file are shortened so, each earlier text verbatim in the history, before batch 8 launches: his choice of option 2 when the growth history showed the batches' rung entries, about 14 KB a landed batch, as most of FACTS' growth. The files read at every boot hold a clean current state and do not need edits as the work moves; the narrative of how a landed rung established a fact is history.
- **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.

    27	## The agents and their prices
    28	
    29	- **How many agents run at once: 2.** The multi-agent harness (the script-driven tool that starts agents in parallel or in sequence) runs two agents at a time on this box; more wait for a free slot.
    30	- **An agent's floor is about 45,000 tokens before it does anything** (system prompt, tools, first message). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (about 33,000 tokens read) and not the first user message (about 11,000 tokens written by each agent). Agents started with an identical whole prompt share the cache (the second reads what the first wrote and writes nothing); a prompt that differs only in its last line shares only the system prompt and tools (about 35,000 tokens read) and writes the rest again.
    31	- **The prompt cache lives 1 hour for the main session and 5 minutes for a subagent.** A call within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait taken in steps shorter than the life costs a cache read per step. A wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again with no cache read: a subagent holding a 250,000-token context that waits 8 minutes on a build writes 250,000 tokens at its next call.
    32	- **The Bash tool's time limit is 10 minutes** (600 s) for a foreground call (default 2 minutes); the call is killed at the limit. A longer command runs in the background and is polled.
    33	- **The project counts cost as tokens written**: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
    34	- **Three model tiers are available: Opus, Sonnet and Fable.** Fable is the strongest and draws on a separate, scarcer weekly pool; Sonnet is the cheapest. An agent that names no model inherits the session's.
    35	- **An agent call can come back empty.** The harness returns null for an agent it has marked failed, even when the agent delivered its structured result first (the platform's safety filter has ended agents this way); a design must expect it.
    36	- **The platform stops the session's process after about 13 hours** (12 h 58 min of continuous running; the stops fall at 46,636 to 46,660 s) and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. The restart kills every running harness run and every running agent; the conversation, the worktrees, the transcripts and each run's journal survive. **A run of the harness is resumed from its journal**: agents that had finished keep their results, an unfinished agent runs again from its start. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's agent calls in call order, so it needs the script and its arguments exactly as at launch and the agents called in the same order. A VM restart and an interrupt of the session's current turn also kill running agents; a resume from the journal recovers the harness's agents that had finished.

56	### The rules for a worker
57	
58	After an edit:
59	
60	- Edited `X.fss` of a library component, and not its `.fsi`: `fortress compile X.fss`, that component alone (CompilerBuiltin about 60 s, CompilerLibrary about 25 s, the others 2 to 16 s). Programs need no recompile.
61	- Edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: all five in library order, about 100 s. Edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: CompilerSystem alone.
62	- Compiling your own program never rebuilds the library. If you skip the step above, a body edit runs the old code with no warning, and an api edit dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
63	- Walk needs nothing: it re-analyses an edited library source on its next run.
64	- Edited Java or Scala: run `ant compileAll` (25 to 40 s on a built tree), then `git checkout -- default_repository/caches/global.map`. Run the library order (about 100 s) only before a compiled run (`fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `junit.sh`). Harness-one, the checker count, the distance stage and the suites use their own caches and need neither.
65	- Do not wipe the cache for any of these.
66	
67	After a failed build:
68	
69	- `ant compileAll` failed: fix the error and run it again. The cache is already gone, because cleanCache runs first; there is nothing else to clear. Then restore `global.map`, and run the library order before any compiled run.
70	- `fortress compile` of a library component failed or was killed: it wrote nothing, or only its jar. Fix the error and compile that component again before any compiled run, because until then programs link its old jar without any warning. Delete nothing.
71	- A `NoSuchMethodError` from a compiled run means a component was not recompiled after an edit or after `ant compileAll`. Recompile the edited component, or run the library order. Do not wipe.

The base build's compiled caches do not hold the api `Executable`, so the compile of any program that exports it parses `Executable.fsi` from source. `*.log` is in `.gitignore`.
132	  - Every cache file the runs wrote went to the private folder. The compile wrote the `.tfs` and jar of `EqualityRung1` and the `.tfi` of `Executable`, and the walk wrote the two entries of `BooleanOps`. No library component was rebuilt. Under the base, the runs read the build, the library sources and `default_repository/configuration`, and never `default_repository/caches`.
133	  - The base's checksum before and after was identical except for one line, the date of the directory `Library/`, which the two logs moved. The checksum covered every file's md5 and every file's and directory's size, date and mode, 23,519 lines with `.git` left out.
134	- Two chains at once, each a compile, a run and a walk with its own private folder and scratch directory, both printed `PASS` and exited 0, in 21.7 s each. Each folder got its own `EqualityRung1.jar`. The checksum was again identical except for the date of `Library/`.
135	  - The two chains wrote their logs beside `Executable.fsi` 0.43 s apart (77 ms and 150 ms windows), so the windows did not overlap in this run.
136	  - When the windows do overlap, the two runs share the two names, and that is harmless. The base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty. A log the other run has already removed reads as empty: `Parser.java:373-377` reads `File.length()`, which is 0 for a missing file.
137	  - A run killed inside the window leaves an empty, ignored log. The seed's clean check reads `git status` and does not see it.
138	- `harness-one.sh` on the old code (`FORTRESS_HOME=<base>`, with its own scratch caches as always) passed in 25.0 s (`OK (1 test)`). It parses the whole library from source, so it created and deleted 58 logs beside 29 library sources and left none. The checksum was identical except for the dates of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`.
139	
140	So this form is safe, and it replaces the per-rung copy. Nothing it writes under the base build stays, and its one transient write, empty logs under shared names, is harmless when two runs overlap. The difference from section 1 is that a seeded copy reads nothing of the base, while this form reads the base build and writes transient logs beside the base's library sources. The new `tools/old-fortress.sh <base build> <private folder> <fortress arguments>` runs it. On first use it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches. It refuses a folder inside the base build, and it runs the base build's `bin/fortress` with both variables set, overriding the worktree's `FORTRESS_HOME` from `env.sh`. A trial compile, run and walk took 17.1 s without `strace`, and a folder inside the base was refused with exit 2.
141	
142	### The dates of the tracked files
143	
144	The script stamped the copied build and caches with one time after the checkout, and it left every tracked file at its checkout date. Git writes files in path order, so `Library/FortressAst.fsi` comes out older than `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`.
145	
146	Ant compares these dates in three places:
147	- makeAST runs when `Fortress.ast` or an astgen source is newer than `nodes/AbstractNode.java` or `Library/FortressAst.fs[is]` (`build.xml:450-467`).
148	- operatorsGen runs when the build's `OperatorStuffGenerator.class` or `Element.class` is newer than `Operators.java` (`:371-384`).
149	- javac recompiles a source newer than its class.
150	
151	In a base built by ant, each generated set is newer than its inputs, because the base's own run regenerated them. In `fortress-base10`, `Fortress.ast` is dated 03:24:15, `FortressAst.fsi` 03:24:35, `AbstractNode.java` 03:24:38, and `Operators.java` 03:24:41, after `OperatorStuffGenerator.class` at 03:24:27.
152	
153	The measurement used two worktrees seeded from `eng-base` at a scratch commit, on no branch, that adds a comment line at the top of `interpreter/glue/prim/FloatLiteral.java`: a branch whose Java differs from the base. In each, a comment line was added at the top of `IntLiteral.java` after seeding, then `ant compileAll` ran. The two runs went one after the other, at load 10:
154	
155	| | script before | script after |
156	|---|---|---|
157	| seed | 2 s | 3 s |
158	| `ant compileAll` | 142.9 s | 77.0 s |
159	| makeAST | ran (`Processing …/Fortress.ast`) | `Nodes up to date? true` |
160	| operatorsGen | ran | `Operators up to date? true` |
161	| javac | 1,077 files | 2 files |
162	| `FloatLiteral.class`, the branch's change | the base's, not recompiled | recompiled |
163	| `IntLiteral.class`, the edit | recompiled | recompiled |
164	
165	Section 2's 38.7 s edit, in which javac recompiled 1,077 of 1,807 files, was this regeneration and not the edit. The Opus engineer measured 104 s against 74 s at load 5 to 8.
166	
167	The `FloatLiteral.class` row is a defect of the old script. A branch whose Java differed from the base was seeded with the build dated after its sources, so `ant compileAll` never recompiled the differing `.java` files. The worker would have run the base's classes for them with no warning, even though the script's warning told it to run `ant compileAll`. Scala was not affected, because scalac recompiles every source on every run.
168	
169	The change, in `tools/seed-worktree.sh`:
170	- The copies of the build, `.dependencies` and the caches keep the base's dates (`cp -a`), and the restamp is gone.
171	- Every tracked file whose content is the base commit's takes the base file's date, to the nanosecond. Git decides which files those are (`git diff --name-only <base>`); the Opus engineer's `mtimesync.py` compared sizes.
172	- Every tracked file that differs from the base's commit, committed or not, and every file the base itself has changed, is stamped two seconds after everything else. This generalizes the old stamp for differing library sources.
173	
174	Every date comparison then comes out as it does in the base, except that the differences are newer than everything copied. The step takes 0.9 to 1.4 s for 7,274 tracked files, including a `git update-index --refresh`, so the worktree's first `git status` does not hash every file again. The caches are still current: in `eng-base`, seeded this way, the compile and the walk above rebuilt no library entry. The base's own dates must be a build's. A base built in place by ant, as the coordinator builds it, qualifies, and so does one seeded by the new script. A base seeded by the old script would pass its checkout dates on.
175	
176	### Keeping the caches through a rebuild: `ant -Dcache0=/nonexistent -Dcache1=/nonexistent compileAll`
177	
178	Read only, not run. `compileAll` depends on `compileCommon`, which depends on `cleanCache` (`build.xml:715`, `:356-360`), and `cleanCache` deletes `${cache0}` (`default_repository/caches`, `:42`) and `${cache1}`. A property given on ant's command line wins over the file's `<property>`, so the command deletes nothing and keeps `global.map` too. Fable saw the caches intact (`cache-sharing.md`, section 2). What it keeps are entries the compiler made before the edit.
179	
180	The repository never checks those entries against the compiler. It judges an entry by the source's date against the entry's (`GraphRepository.java:243-244`, `:282-283`) and by a hash of the foreign Java signatures the source imports (`:531-533`). It never looks at the compiler's own classes. A kept entry is therefore used without warning, and since a `fortress compile` of an unchanged source writes nothing and exits 0 (rung 7's trap, noted under the batch script's library order), the library order does not rebuild it either. Once kept, a stale entry stays until the caches are deleted.
181	
182	The build file states the rule the flag bypasses: "Whenever any part of the compiler source code is recompiled, we need to clean the cache because we can't ensure that existing target code is still valid (or even sensical)" (`build.xml:711-713`). The gate is not exposed to the kept caches: `testFast` and `testSystem` delete their private caches before they run (`:964`, `:1205`), and harness-one, the checker count and the distance stage use their own (section 2). The kept caches reach only the worker's own compiled runs, `junit.sh` and direct walk runs.
183	
184	- **Safe:** an edit that cannot change any cached form. That means walk's evaluator and its natives (`interpreter/evaluator`, `interpreter/glue`), the bodies of the run-time classes that compiled code calls (`runtimeSystem`, `compiler/runtimeValues`) with no change to a signature, or code that no compile or run uses (the test harness, `Shell`'s options). The flag saves the library order, about 100 s (section 2), and the restore of `global.map`.
185	- **The library must be recompiled:** after an edit to anything the library's compile runs. That covers the parser and the AST (`Fortress.ast`, the generated nodes and their serialization), the disambiguator, the static checker (the Java and Scala type checkers, overloading, exclusion), the desugarers, and the code generator (`compiler/codegen`, `NamingCzar`, `OverloadSet`). It also covers a changed signature of a run-time class the jars call, and for walk, its rewriting passes (`interpreter/rewrite`). Most climb rungs edit the checker or the code generator.
186	
187	Recommendation: plain `ant compileAll` stays the rule after a Java or Scala edit. The flag can be offered only for an edit confined to the safe list, by a worker who names the edited files against that list. It is not built in.
188	
189	## For Pavol
190	
191	Yes, the build can be shared. One finished build is copied into each new work tree in about 3 seconds, and the copy fixes the places where the folder's location is written into the saved results. Fortress accepts the copy and rebuilds nothing. Programs and tests give the same results as in the original, and the copy never reads the original's files. The 3 to 7 minutes each rung, skeptic and repair spent rebuilding goes away.
192	
193	Fortress does notice edits, but only when you compile the part you edited: compiling your own program does not rebuild the library under it. If that step is skipped, the run either uses the old code without saying so or crashes with a missing-method error. A wipe is never the fix; recompiling the edited part is.
194	
195	In batch 8, the four rungs each built the same starting point, and the skeptics and one repair rebuilt states the workers had already built. After the review's repair, which changed only specification text, the whole 25-minute gate ran again with the same result. That is about 107 minutes and 230K tokens of repeated work. One build at the launch, a copy per worktree, and skipping the gate when no code changed remove all of it.
196	
197	Added on 2026-10-03: the two engineers' cheaper ways hold up. The old code now runs straight from the one base build, with a private 36 MB copy of its saved results made in a twentieth of a second, instead of a 206 MB copy of the whole tree per rung; that writes nothing that stays in the base, and two runs at once do not disturb each other. Seeded worktrees now also take the base's file dates, so the first Java edit no longer regenerates a thousand generated files: 77 s instead of 143 s. That change also fixed a defect, in which a branch's own Java changes were silently not recompiled. Keeping the saved results through a Java rebuild is safe only for edits that cannot change how the library compiles, which excludes most climb rungs, so it stays optional.
